const NestedPalettes = () => (
  <Theme appearance="dark" accentColor="orange" grayColor="slate" data-testid="dark" style={{ background: 'var(--color-surface)', padding: 'var(--space-4)' }}>
    <Theme appearance="light" style={{ background: 'var(--color-surface)', padding: 'var(--space-4)' }}>
      <Theme accentColor="orange" grayColor="slate" data-testid="island">
        <Panel label="orange on slate, light, inside dark" />
        <Theme appearance="dark" style={{ padding: 'var(--space-2)' }}>
          <Theme accentColor="orange" grayColor="slate" data-testid="deep">
            <Panel label="and dark again inside that" />
          </Theme>
        </Theme>
      </Theme>
      <Theme accentColor="orange" grayColor="slate" appearance="dark" data-testid="same-element">
        <Panel label="accent and appearance on one element" />
      </Theme>
    </Theme>
  </Theme>
);
stories.description:
An accent or gray set on a light island inside a dark page takes the
island's appearance, not the page's: the nearest scope wins at any depth.

foundations-overview--docs.title: Foundations/Overview
foundations-overview--docs.content:
import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as OverviewStories from './Overview.stories'

<Meta of={OverviewStories} />

# Foundations

Foundations are the decisions every component inherits: color, type,
spacing, radius, elevation, cursors, and the breakpoints layouts respond
to. They live in **one file** — `src/tokens.css` — as CSS custom
properties.

There is no JavaScript theme object and no `ThemeProvider` that owns
values. A token is a CSS variable, which means the platform already knows
how to scope it, cascade it, inherit it and override it. Everything on
this page follows from that.

`tokens.css` is itself generated — see [Where the values come
from](#where-the-values-come-from) — but nothing downstream of it is.
**You** consume a plain stylesheet with no build step of your own.

## The three layers

| Layer | Where | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Raw value | `:root` / `.dark` in `tokens.css` | `--color-background-brand-bold: oklch(51.1% 0.262 276.966)` |
| Derived value | the `*` block in `tokens.css` | `--radius-control: max(…)` |
| Usage | a component's `.module.css` | `background: var(--color-background-brand-bold)` |

Components only ever read the variable. That is what makes a rebrand a
change to one file, and what keeps theme conditionals out of component CSS
entirely — the value behind `var(--color-background-brand-bold)` changes, the rule does not.

The derived layer is on `*` rather than `:root` on purpose: a custom
property that reads another one resolves where it is *declared*, so
putting these at the root would freeze them there and a `Theme` further
down the tree could not move them.

## Where the values come from

`tokens.css` is not written by hand. The source is a set of JSON files in
the [W3C design-token format](https://tr.designtokens.org/format/), and a
generator turns them into the stylesheet, the `Theme` component's list of
palettes, the swatches on the **Color** page, and an export for design
tools — four artefacts that used to be four chances to disagree with each
other.

Two things follow from that, and both are visible on other pages here.

**Nothing semantic holds a literal.** In the source,
`color-background-brand-bold` is `{accent.solid}` and `color-text` is
`{gray.950}` — references, not colours. Swapping a ramp moves everything downstream of it in one edit,
which is what makes the 17 accents and 9 grays on this page a
three-line change rather than a rewrite.

**The contrast numbers are measured, not claimed.** For each of the 17
accents the generator converts the ramp through OKLCH → sRGB → relative
luminance, computes the contrast of each candidate step against a white
and a black label, and takes the first that clears 4.5:1. The focus ring
is a separate measurement against the page at 3:1. The lowest passing
accent in the current set sits at **4.56:1** — close enough to the floor
that guessing would have missed it.

Edit a ramp so that no step can carry a readable label and the build
stops with the hue named. The accessibility claims on the
[Color](?path=/docs/foundations-colors--docs) page are therefore checks,
not documentation.

## The pages

- **[Color](?path=/docs/foundations-colors--docs)** — semantic tokens, the
  contrast measurements, and where every value comes from.
- **[Dark mode](?path=/docs/foundations-dark-mode--docs)** — how the two
  modes are declared and switched.
- **[Typography](?path=/docs/foundations-typography--docs)** — the
  role-based type scale, and the system font stack behind it.
- **[Spacing](?path=/docs/foundations-spacing--docs)** — six roles,
  one value each.
- **[Breakpoints](?path=/docs/foundations-breakpoints--docs)** — the
  responsive range, and the kit's lack of opinion about it.
- **[Radius](?path=/docs/foundations-radius--docs)** — four steps off one
  base, and what happens at the extremes.
- **[Shadows](?path=/docs/foundations-shadows--docs)** — elevation, and why
  dark mode needs its own alphas.
- **[Focus](?path=/docs/foundations-focus--docs)** — one ring, two
  offsets, and when to draw it inside.
- **[Motion](?path=/docs/foundations-motion--docs)** — three transition
  durations, one spinner speed, and reduced motion in one place.
- **[Layering](?path=/docs/foundations-layering--docs)** — four layers,
  and why every overlay shares one.
- **[Cursors](?path=/docs/foundations-cursors--docs)** — two tokens and one
  contested convention.

## Theming

Overriding tokens globally is just CSS — redeclare them after Zweihänder's
stylesheet loads:

```css
:root {
  --radius: 1rem;
  --color-background-brand-bold: oklch(0.55 0.2 264);
}
```

For anything narrower than the whole document, use `Theme`. It is a thin
wrapper that applies an appearance class and writes token overrides as
inline custom properties on one element, so everything inside it resolves
against those values.

```tsx
import { Theme } from 'zweihander/theme'

<Theme accentColor="violet" grayColor="slate" appearance="dark" radius="full-rounded">
  <Button>Inside a violet, slate, dark, rounder scope</Button>
</Theme>
```

Four settings, each independent:

| Prop | Values |
| --- | --- |
| `accentColor` | 17 hues — drives the brand tokens (`--color-background-brand-bold`, `--color-text-brand`, `--color-icon-brand`) and `--color-border-focused` |
| `grayColor` | 9 neutral ramps — drives backgrounds, text, borders |
| `appearance` | `light`, `dark`, `inherit` |
| `radius` | `sharp`, `rounded`, `full-rounded` |

### Accent color

The brand hue. Seventeen, all of them measured: the solid step and the
label colour are chosen per hue so every accent clears 4.5:1 for its own
label, which is why the warm hues below carry dark labels and the cool
ones carry white. The focus ring uses a step darker than the fill, because
the lighter solids miss the 3:1 a focus indicator needs.

<Canvas of={OverviewStories.AccentColor} />

### Gray color

The neutral ramp behind surfaces, text, borders and neutral fills. The
differences are subtle and cumulative; they read most clearly in dark
mode, which is how they are shown here.

<Canvas of={OverviewStories.GrayColor} />

### Radius

Covered on its own page, including why `full` pills a button but not a
text field: **[Radius](?path=/docs/foundations-radius--docs)**.

### Appearance

`appearance` takes `light`, `dark`, or `inherit` (the default, which
leaves the surrounding mode alone).

<Canvas of={OverviewStories.Appearance} />

### Token overrides

`tokens` takes any custom property, with or without the `--` prefix. It is
not limited to tokens Zweihänder defines — the component writes whatever
you pass onto the element, so a token your own components read works the
same way.

<Canvas of={OverviewStories.TokenOverride} />

Overrides cascade, so a nested `Theme` inherits what it does not restate.
Because they are inline styles they also beat any stylesheet rule, which
is what makes a scoped override reliable — and what makes `Theme` the
wrong tool for setting global defaults. Use CSS for those.

### Nesting

Scopes nest in either direction: a dark panel on a light page, or a light
island inside a dark one.

<Canvas of={OverviewStories.Nested} />

The light island works because `tokens.css` declares the light values on
`:root, .light`, not on `:root` alone. `.dark` is declared afterwards at
equal specificity, so the nearer scope's class is what an element inside
it resolves against.

An `accentColor` or `grayColor` inside a nested scope follows the same
rule. Each appearance sets two switches, `--use-light` and `--use-dark`,
and the palette scopes pick their light or dark values through them, so
the nearest appearance wins at any depth, on the same element too.

<Canvas of={OverviewStories.NestedPalettes} />

**One caveat.** If your own CSS branches on theme with a descendant
selector (`.dark .thing { … }`), that selector still matches inside a
light island nested in a dark ancestor, and will style it as dark.
Zweihänder's own CSS never branches on theme, so it is unaffected. Read
the tokens instead of matching on `.dark` and the problem does not arise.

## Installing

Both distribution paths carry the same tokens. Copy-source drops the
component's own source into your repo and merges these values into your
stylesheet; the npm package ships them as `zweihander/tokens.css`, which
you import after your base stylesheet.

The exact commands for either are in the
[repo README](https://github.com/nguucode/zweihander).

foundations-colors--docs.content:
import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as ColorsStories from './Colors.stories'

<Meta of={ColorsStories} />

# Colors

Every color in the system is a CSS custom property declared in
`src/tokens.css`, with a counterpart under the `.dark` class. The source is
`tokens/semantic.json`; `npm run tokens` generates the stylesheet from it
and measures the contrast pairs listed below. One stylesheet holds both
modes, so a rule that reads `var(--color-text)` switches theme without a
conditional.

**The swatches on this page read their values out of the live document**,
so a color shown here is the value the components get. The token *names*
are listed by hand in `Colors.stories.tsx`.

## Naming

Names follow Atlassian's design tokens:

```
--color-<category>-<role>[-<emphasis>]
```

The **category** says what the color is painted on: `surface`, `text`,
`icon`, `border`, `background`, `interaction`, `blanket` or `chart`. Pick
the category by the CSS property you are setting — a `color` on a label is
a `text` token, a `fill` on a glyph is an `icon` token, a `background` on a
button is a `background` token. The bare category (`--color-text`,
`--color-border`) is the default for it.

The **role** says what it means: `brand`, `neutral`, `input`, `selected`,
a status (`info`, `success`, `warning`, `danger`), or `accent-<hue>`.

The **emphasis** says how strong it is, from weakest to strongest:
`subtlest`, `subtle`, (none), `bold`, `bolder`. `-inverse` is text or an
icon that sits on a `bold` fill of the same role.

In Figma the Color collection mirrors this as `<category>/<role>`:
`text/subtlest`, `background/brand-bold`, and `text/default` for the bare
`--color-text`. Each variable's code syntax is its `var(--color-…)`, so
Dev Mode shows the CSS name.

## Surfaces

What a region of the page is. `--color-surface` is the page;
`--color-surface-raised` is a card or panel set into it;
`--color-surface-overlay` is anything that floats above it — a menu,
popover, modal or toast. In light mode the page is gray-50 and the two
raised surfaces are white, so a panel separates by being lighter and needs
a border at most. In dark mode the page is the darkest step and both
raised surfaces are lifted one step toward the viewer.

| Token | Role | Light | Dark |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--color-surface` | The page | gray-50 | gray-950 |
| `--color-surface-raised` | A card or panel in the page | white | gray-900 |
| `--color-surface-overlay` | A menu, popover, modal or toast | white | gray-900 |

Text on any surface is `--color-text` (or a quieter text token below).
There is no per-surface foreground: one text token works on all three.

<Canvas of={ColorsStories.Surfaces} />

## Text

| Token | Role | Light | Dark |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--color-text` | Body text, headings, labels | gray-950 | gray-50 |
| `--color-text-subtle` | Text that recedes until hovered or current: navigation labels | gray-600 | gray-300 |
| `--color-text-subtlest` | Secondary text: descriptions, hints, captions, placeholders | gray-500 | gray-400 |
| `--color-text-inverse` | Text on `--color-background-neutral-bold` | gray-50 | gray-50 |
| `--color-text-brand` | Brand-coloured text: an outlined or ghost primary button, a link | accent text step | accent text step |
| `--color-text-brand-bold` | Text on `--color-background-brand-subtlest` | accent-800 or darker | accent-300 or lighter |
| `--color-text-brand-inverse` | Label on `--color-background-brand-bold` | white or near-black, per accent | near-black |
| `--color-text-<status>` | Status text on the page or on its tint | 800 | 300 |
| `--color-text-<status>-inverse` | Label on `--color-background-<status>-bold` | neutral-50 (warning: neutral-900) | neutral-900 |
| `--color-text-accent-<hue>` | Hue text on the page or on its tint | 800 | 300 |
| `--color-text-accent-<hue>-inverse` | Label on `--color-background-accent-<hue>-bolder` | neutral-50 | neutral-50 |

`--color-text-subtle` is body-safe (7.24:1 on the light page). Use
`--color-text-subtlest` for genuinely secondary text; it still clears 4.5:1
on every surface and fill it is allowed on (see Contrast).

`--color-text-brand` is a separate step from the brand fill. The fill is
picked so its label reads; read as text on the page, amber-500 is barely
2:1, so the build picks the first step of the accent that clears 4.5:1
against the page instead.

## Icons

Glyphs take `icon` tokens, not `text` tokens. They are separate so an icon
can sit at a different step from the text beside it: a status icon is the
saturated hue, its text the darker 800 step.

| Token | Role | Light | Dark |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--color-icon` | Default glyph | gray-950 | gray-50 |
| `--color-icon-subtle` | A glyph that recedes: a chevron, a field's leading icon | gray-500 | gray-400 |
| `--color-icon-inverse` | A glyph on a bold neutral fill | gray-50 | gray-50 |
| `--color-icon-brand` | A brand-coloured glyph | accent text step | accent text step |
| `--color-icon-info` | Info glyph | blue-600 | blue-400 |
| `--color-icon-success` | Success glyph | green-700 | green-400 |
| `--color-icon-warning` | Warning glyph | amber-600 | amber-400 |
| `--color-icon-danger` | Danger glyph | red-600 | red-400 |

## Borders

| Token | Role | Light | Dark |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--color-border` | A divider or container edge | gray-200 | white 10% |
| `--color-border-input` | A text field's edge | gray-300 | white 18% |
| `--color-border-bold` | A checkbox, radio or switch track outline | gray-500 | gray-400 |
| `--color-border-focused` | The focus indicator | accent-700 | accent-400 |

Choose by what the edge has to do. `--color-border` separates things and
is never the only sign something is there. `--color-border-input` is the
light hairline of a text field: about 1.5:1, a deliberate exception to 3:1
because a field also has its label, placeholder, fill and focus ring. A
product that needs 3:1 on fields sets
`--color-border-input: var(--color-border-bold)`. `--color-border-bold` is
for controls that have nothing else showing they are there, so it clears
3:1 against the page (WCAG 1.4.11). `--color-border-focused` follows the
accent one step darker than its fill, because the lighter solids miss 3:1
against the page — yellow-600 measures 2.93:1.

In dark mode the two lighter borders are translucent white, so an edge
reads the same on `--color-surface` and on a lifted
`--color-surface-raised`.

<Canvas of={ColorsStories.LinesAndFocus} />

## Backgrounds

Fills behind content that is not a surface: a button, a selected row, a
filled field, a status message.

| Token | Role | Light | Dark |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--color-background-neutral` | A quiet fill: secondary button, a disabled field, a zebra stripe | gray-100 | gray-800 |
| `--color-background-neutral-bold` | A solid neutral fill (a neutral Avatar) | gray-600 | gray-600 |
| `--color-background-selected` | The current item: a selected row, the active nav item | gray-200 | white 10% |
| `--color-background-input` | A filled panel or field that subtlest text can sit on | gray-50 | gray-800 |
| `--color-background-brand-bold` | The default button: **the brand hue** | accent solid | accent solid |
| `--color-background-brand-subtlest` | A brand tint | accent-100 | accent-950 |
| `--color-background-<status>-bold` | Solid status fill | 600 (success 700, warning 500) | 400 |
| `--color-background-<status>` | Status tint | 100 | 950 |
| `--color-background-accent-<hue>-bolder` | Solid hue fill (a solid Tag) | 600 | 600 |
| `--color-background-accent-<hue>-subtler` | Hue tint | 100 | 950 |

`--color-background-brand-bold` is the one fill the
[`accentColor`](?path=/docs/foundations-overview--docs) setting moves, with
`--color-text-brand`, `--color-icon-brand`, the brand tint and
`--color-border-focused`. The accent solid is step 600 for most hues and
700 for sky, fuchsia, pink and rose in light mode, and its label is white
or near-black, whichever clears 4.5:1 on it.

<Canvas of={ColorsStories.SubtleSurfaces} />

<Canvas of={ColorsStories.SolidActions} />

## Interaction, blanket

| Token | Role | Light | Dark |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--color-interaction-hovered` | Hover overlay, laid over whatever fill the item already has | black 5% | white 6% |
| `--color-blanket` | Behind a modal | black 50% | black 50% |

`--color-interaction-hovered` is translucent so one token works on any
surface or fill: lay it on top (a second background layer or a
pseudo-element), do not swap the fill for it.

## Status and hue

Four status roles carry meaning about state: `info` (blue), `success`
(green), `warning` (amber), `danger` (red). They are fixed hues and do not
follow the accent: a status colour that changes with the brand stops being
a status. Each role has a solid fill and its label, a tint, text that reads
on the tint or the page, and an icon:

```
--color-background-<status>-bold   --color-text-<status>-inverse
--color-background-<status>        --color-text-<status>
--color-icon-<status>
```

`danger` is also the destructive action: a delete button is
`--color-background-danger-bold` with `--color-text-danger-inverse`. If the
accent is already red, tell a destructive action apart by wording and
placement, not by colour alone.

The 17 hues (`red` to `rose`, as in the primitives below) carry category,
not state — a Tag colour, an Avatar's initials. Each has a solid, its
label, a tint, and text:

```
--color-background-accent-<hue>-bolder   --color-text-accent-<hue>-inverse
--color-background-accent-<hue>-subtler  --color-text-accent-<hue>
```

Every hue's solid is step 600 with a white label in both modes, so a row of
solid tags reads as one set. The warm hues fall below 4.5:1 there, and the
build does not measure hue labels on purpose (decision of 2026-10-08).
`--color-text-accent-orange-contrast` is a near-black label (neutral-900)
for orange, for a place that has to pass 4.5:1 on the orange solid; nothing
in the kit reads it yet.

## Chart

`--color-chart-1` to `--color-chart-8` colour series in the charts, in
order. They are separate from the hue tokens so the series order can be
tuned for neighbours that stay distinguishable.

| Token | Light | Dark |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--color-chart-1` | blue-600 | blue-400 |
| `--color-chart-2` | yellow-700 | yellow-400 |
| `--color-chart-3` | pink-600 | pink-400 |
| `--color-chart-4` | teal-600 | teal-500 |
| `--color-chart-5` | violet-600 | violet-400 |
| `--color-chart-6` | orange-600 | orange-500 |
| `--color-chart-7` | cyan-600 | cyan-500 |
| `--color-chart-8` | lime-700 | lime-500 |

## Contrast

Measured, not assumed. `npm run tokens` computes each pair below from the
OKLCH values and stops the build if one drops under its floor. WCAG AA
wants 4.5:1 for text and 3:1 for the edge of a control or a chart mark.

- **Brand labels:** for each of the 17 accents, the solid and its label are
  picked together so `--color-text-brand-inverse` clears 4.5:1 on
  `--color-background-brand-bold`. `--color-text-brand` clears 4.5:1
  against the page, and `--color-border-focused` clears 3:1 against it.
- **Status:** for each of info, success, warning and danger, in both modes,
  `--color-text-<status>-inverse` on the bold fill, and
  `--color-text-<status>` on its tint and on the page, all at 4.5:1.
- **Hues:** `--color-text-accent-<hue>` on its subtler tint and on the
  page, at 4.5:1. Labels on the bolder fill are not measured (see above).
- **Secondary text:** `--color-text-subtlest` on `--color-surface`,
  `--color-surface-raised`, `--color-background-input` and
  `--color-background-neutral`, at 4.5:1 on all nine gray ramps in both
  modes.
- **Neutral solid:** `--color-text-inverse` on
  `--color-background-neutral-bold`, at 4.5:1 on all nine gray ramps.
- **Control outlines:** `--color-border-bold` against the page, at 3:1 on
  all nine gray ramps.
- **Chart marks:** each `--color-chart-<n>` against `--color-surface-raised`,
  at 3:1 on all nine gray ramps. This is why yellow and lime take step 700
  in light.

The values on the defaults (blue accent, gray ramp):

| Pair | Light | Dark |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--color-text` on `--color-surface` | 19.28:1 | 19.28:1 |
| `--color-text` on `--color-surface-raised` | 20.13:1 | 17.00:1 |
| `--color-text-subtle` on `--color-surface` | 7.24:1 | 13.67:1 |
| `--color-text-subtlest` on `--color-surface` | 4.85:1 | 7.73:1 |
| `--color-text-subtlest` on `--color-background-neutral` | 4.60:1 | 5.64:1 |
| `--color-text-brand-inverse` on `--color-background-brand-bold` | 5.03:1 | 6.79:1 |
| `--color-text-brand` on `--color-surface` | 5.04:1 | 7.63:1 |
| `--color-text-inverse` on `--color-background-neutral-bold` | 7.24:1 | 7.24:1 |
| `--color-border-focused` on `--color-surface` | 6.54:1 | 7.63:1 |
| `--color-border-bold` on `--color-surface` | 4.85:1 | 7.73:1 |

| Status pair | info | success | warning | danger |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| label on bold, light | 5.03:1 | 4.73:1 | 8.35:1 | 4.56:1 |
| text on tint, light | 7.25:1 | 6.45:1 | 6.41:1 | 6.86:1 |
| text on page, light | 8.47:1 | 6.80:1 | 6.83:1 | 8.02:1 |
| label on bold, dark | 6.79:1 | 10.09:1 | 10.43:1 | 6.19:1 |
| text on tint, dark | 8.13:1 | 10.67:1 | 10.37:1 | 8.40:1 |
| text on page, dark | 11.11:1 | 14.40:1 | 13.92:1 | 10.48:1 |

The tightest pair is `--color-text-subtlest` on
`--color-background-neutral` in light mode, at 4.60:1: gray-500 on every
ramp is the lightest value that clears 4.6:1 on its own gray-100. Dark
`--color-text-danger-inverse` is neutral-900, not near-white: the danger
fill lightens to red-400 in dark mode, and near-white on red-400 is 2.77:1.

## Color is never the only signal

`--color-background-danger-bold` on a button does not say what will be
destroyed, and a red tag means nothing to a reader who cannot tell it from
a neutral one. Pair colour with words, an icon or a shape every time it
carries meaning. The numbers above are a floor, not a design review.

## Dark mode

Every token has a counterpart under `.dark`, switched by a class. Dark is
not an inversion of light: surfaces go *up*, and strong fills get lighter
so their labels flip to dark text. The mechanism and how to follow the OS
setting are on their own page:
**[Dark mode](?path=/docs/foundations-dark-mode--docs)**.

## Primitives

The palette underneath: 17 hues and 9 gray ramps, 11 shades each. Two ramps feed the semantic
tokens and each can be swapped on its own: an **accent** (blue by default)
for the brand tokens, and a **gray** (`gray` by default) for surfaces,
text, borders and neutral fills. The status, hue and chart tokens pin
their own ramps. The exceptions to "every value is a ramp step" are the
white raised surfaces in light mode and the translucent tokens: the dark
borders, dark selected fill, hover overlay and blanket.

This is raw material, not a palette to build UI from. Reach for a
primitive when you are defining the *next* semantic token; if a primitive
shows up in a component, a token is missing. The classes are generated by
an `@source inline(...)` directive in `src/index.css` only so this page
can render them.

<Canvas of={ColorsStories.Primitives} />

## Migrating from 0.8

0.9.0 renamed every colour token and removed the old names. The main ones:

{/* docs:check allow --background --card --popover --foreground --card-foreground --popover-foreground --secondary-foreground --accent-foreground --muted-foreground --subtle-foreground --primary --primary-foreground --primary-text --secondary --muted --accent --selected --surface-filled --border --input --field-border --control-border --ring --destructive --destructive-foreground --neutral-solid --neutral-solid-foreground --hover-overlay --scrim --warning-indicator -- old 0.8 names, listed for migration */}

| 0.8 | 0.9 |
| --- | --- |
| `--background` | `--color-surface` |
| `--card` | `--color-surface-raised` |
| `--popover` | `--color-surface-overlay` |
| `--foreground`, `--card-foreground`, `--popover-foreground`, `--secondary-foreground`, `--accent-foreground` | `--color-text` |
| `--subtle-foreground` | `--color-text-subtle` |
| `--muted-foreground` | `--color-text-subtlest` |
| `--primary` | `--color-background-brand-bold` |
| `--primary-foreground` | `--color-text-brand-inverse` |
| `--primary-text` | `--color-text-brand` |
| `--secondary`, `--muted`, `--accent` | `--color-background-neutral` |
| `--selected` | `--color-background-selected` |
| `--surface-filled` | `--color-background-input` |
| `--neutral-solid`, `--neutral-solid-foreground` | `--color-background-neutral-bold`, `--color-text-inverse` |
| `--border`, `--input` | `--color-border` |
| `--field-border` | `--color-border-input` |
| `--control-border` | `--color-border-bold` |
| `--ring` | `--color-border-focused` |
| `--destructive`, `--destructive-foreground` | `--color-background-danger-bold`, `--color-text-danger-inverse` |
| `--hover-overlay` | `--color-interaction-hovered` |
| `--scrim` | `--color-blanket` |
| `--warning-indicator` | `--color-icon-warning` |
| --<status>, --<status>-foreground | `--color-background-<status>-bold`, `--color-text-<status>-inverse` |
| --<status>-subtle, --<status>-text | `--color-background-<status>`, `--color-text-<status>` |
| --<hue>, --<hue>-foreground | `--color-background-accent-<hue>-bolder`, `--color-text-accent-<hue>-inverse` |
| --<hue>-subtle, --<hue>-text | `--color-background-accent-<hue>-subtler`, `--color-text-accent-<hue>` |
| --chart-N | `--color-chart-<n>` |

Glyphs that used a text token now have their own: `--color-icon`,
`--color-icon-subtle` and the status icons.

## Customization

Redeclare a token after Zweihänder's stylesheet, or edit
`tokens/semantic.json` and run `npm run tokens` if you own the source.
Nothing that reads `var(--color-background-brand-bold)` changes, because
every rule points at the variable rather than the value.

Two things to carry through a rebrand: re-measure the pairs above — a
brand hue at the same lightness as another will not hit the same ratios —
and keep light and dark as separate decisions. Reusing the light value of
a fill in dark mode is what produced the 2.77:1 failure described under
Contrast.

Projects that install through the registry get these values merged into
their own stylesheet; projects on the npm package import
`zweihander/tokens.css` and override afterwards.

foundations-dark-mode--docs.content:
import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as DarkModeStories from './DarkMode.stories'

<Meta of={DarkModeStories} />

# Dark mode

Dark mode is **a class, not a media query.** `tokens.css` declares the
light values on `:root, .light` and the dark values on `.dark`, and
every rule in the kit reads those variables, so the class is the only
switch there is. The same scopes set `color-scheme`, so the UI the browser
draws itself (scrollbars, date and select popups, autofill) switches with
them.

Nothing is automatic about it. Adding `class="dark"` to `<html>` is what
switches the document; without that, a device set to dark mode gets the
light theme. That is the trade — see **Following the system** below.

<Canvas of={DarkModeStories.SideBySide} />

## Components don't know about it

No component stylesheet — `Button.module.css`, `InputField.module.css` or any other — mentions `.dark`.
They write `background: var(--color-background-brand-bold)`, and it is the variable that
changes; the rule is identical in both modes.

This is the main reason to reach for a token rather than a literal. A
hard-coded `#0a0a0a` is near-black in both modes and needs a `.dark`
override beside it to survive a theme switch; `var(--color-background-brand-bold)` needs
nothing. Every theme conditional in a codebase is a place a value was
hardcoded and then patched.

## Dark is not an inversion

Flipping lightness would produce the wrong result in three places, and the
palette deliberately doesn't:

- **`--color-surface` is gray-950, not black.** A pure-black page makes
  the halation around light text worse and leaves no room to sit a surface
  *below* the page level.
- **Surfaces go up, not down.** `--color-surface-raised` and
  `--color-surface-overlay` are a step *lighter* than the page in dark
  mode (gray-900 on gray-950), as they are in light mode (white on
  gray-50). Elevation in dark mode is carried by lightness, because a drop shadow
  has almost nothing left to darken (see
  [Shadows](?path=/docs/foundations-shadows--docs)).
- **Strong fills become light, so their labels become dark.**
  `--color-background-brand-bold` goes from the accent's 600 step to its
  400, and `--color-text-brand-inverse` turns near-black with it.
  `--color-background-danger-bold` does the same, red-600 to red-400 —
  which is exactly where the palette's one contrast bug lived: keeping the
  near-white `--color-text-danger-inverse` on the lightened red measured
  2.77:1. It is now neutral-900 at 6.19:1. Lightening a fill without
  flipping its `-inverse` label is the single easiest dark-mode mistake to
  make.

Full measurements for both modes are in
[Color → Contrast](?path=/docs/foundations-colors--docs).

## Alpha for edges

`--color-border` and `--color-border-input` are opaque gray-200 and
gray-300 in light, and `white / 10%` and `white / 18%` in dark;
`--color-background-selected` is `white / 10%` in dark too. An opaque dark
border would have to be re-chosen for every surface it sits on; a
translucent white edge lightens whatever is underneath, so the same token
reads correctly on `--color-surface` and on a lifted
`--color-surface-raised`. `--color-interaction-hovered` and
`--color-blanket` are translucent in both modes for the same reason.

## Scoping

`Theme` switches an appearance for a subtree rather than the document —
a dark footer on a light page, a light popover inside a dark shell. See
[Overview → Nesting](?path=/docs/foundations-overview--docs) for how the
nesting resolves and the one caveat that comes with it.

```tsx
<Theme appearance="dark">
  <Footer />
</Theme>
```

## Following the system

The kit ships no `prefers-color-scheme` handling, because the choice
between "follow the OS" and "remember what the user picked" belongs to the
app, not the component library. The usual shape:

```ts
const media = window.matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)')
const stored = localStorage.getItem('theme') // 'light' | 'dark' | null
const dark = stored ? stored === 'dark' : media.matches
document.documentElement.classList.toggle('dark', dark)
```

Two things worth getting right. Run it **before first paint** — in a
blocking inline script in `<head>`, not in a `useEffect` — or the page
renders light and flips, which is the flash every themed site has had at
some point. And keep listening to `media` afterwards so a user changing
their OS setting mid-session is followed, unless they have made an
explicit choice.

In this Storybook, the **Theme** toolbar control does the class toggle for
you; there is no persistence and no system detection.

foundations-typography--docs.content:
import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as TypographyStories from './Typography.stories'

<Meta of={TypographyStories} />

# Typography

Type is **role-based**: you reach for `--text-heading-lg` or `--text-body`,
not a size. Each role carries its size, line height and weight together, so a
heading cannot end up at body weight or a body line height by omission.

The alternative — a purely dimensional scale, where a name says how big and
never what it is for — is what this replaces. Each role is three variables
that belong together:

```css
.heading {
  font-size: var(--text-heading-lg);
  line-height: var(--leading-heading-lg);
  font-weight: 600;
}
```

## The typeface

One face: the platform UI font. Nothing is downloaded, and text looks the
way the rest of the operating system does — San Francisco on Apple, Segoe UI
on Windows, Roboto on Android.

```css
--font-sans: system-ui, -apple-system, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, …
--font-mono: ui-monospace, SFMono-Regular, 'SF Mono', Menlo, …
```

Components read two role tokens rather than the face directly, so a
product can give headings or prose their own face without touching a
component:

| Role | Default | Read by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--font-heading` | `var(--font-sans)` | Page titles, `Modal` and `EmptyState` titles |
| `--font-prose` | `var(--font-sans)` | long-form reading text; no component reads it yet |

<Canvas of={TypographyStories.Families} />

**There is nothing to load.** To use a brand face instead, load it yourself
and point the tokens at it (see **Customization**).

## Headings

Seven steps, all semibold (600). The line height tightens as the size grows, which
is the thing a single ratio applied across a whole scale gets wrong.

<Canvas of={TypographyStories.Headings} />

| Role | Size | Line height |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--text-heading-2xl` | 2rem / 32px | 36px |
| `--text-heading-xl` | 1.75rem / 28px | 32px |
| `--text-heading-lg` | 1.5rem / 24px | 28px |
| `--text-heading-md` | 1.25rem / 20px | 24px |
| `--text-heading-sm` | 1rem / 16px | 20px |
| `--text-heading-xs` | 0.875rem / 14px | 20px |
| `--text-heading-2xs` | 0.75rem / 12px | 16px |

Note that headings go *below* body size: `--text-heading-2xs` is 12px. Those
bottom steps are for labels and section eyebrows — a heading role is about
the semantic weight of the text, not about being large.

## Body

Three steps. `--text-body` is the default at 14px — one step down from the
16px a lot of interfaces start at, which is deliberate for dense product
UI and worth knowing before you reach for it in long-form content.

<Canvas of={TypographyStories.Body} />

| Role | Size | Line height |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--text-body-lg` | 1rem / 16px | 24px |
| `--text-body` | 0.875rem / 14px | 20px |
| `--text-body-sm` | 0.75rem / 12px | 16px |

**Every component uses these.** Button, the field label, the input itself,
and the helper and error text are all `--text-body`; only the large Button
steps up to `--text-body-lg`.

`--text-body-sm` is the label of every small control (the `sm` and `xs`
size tiers, see [Sizing](?path=/docs/foundations-sizing--docs)), and
secondary text: helper text in a menu, shortcuts, captions.

12px is the smallest text size in the kit. `--text-body-xs` used to be
11px; it is now the same as `--text-body-sm` and deprecated, kept so
existing styles keep working.

Every body line height is a multiple of 4px (24, 20, 16), so body text
of any size sits on the same 4px grid as the spacing and control heights.

## Weights

Four. Anything outside this set is not part of the system.

<Canvas of={TypographyStories.Weights} />

| Weight | Value |
| --- | --- |
| regular | 400 |
| medium | 500 |
| semibold | 600 |
| bold | 700 |

Headings are semibold (600). A label beside an icon, such as a button's
or a tab's, is medium (500).

{/* docs:check allow --font-weight-medium -- the paragraph explains why weights are not tokens */}

Weight is written directly rather than tokenised — there are four of them
and they are the same four everywhere, so a `--font-weight-medium`
indirection would buy nothing. The one exception is `--font-weight-label`
(653), a field's label, which a variable face draws between medium and
semibold. Button is `--text-body` at `font-weight:
500`; the role supplies the size and line height, the rule supplies the
weight.

With a system stack, the weight you ask for is not guaranteed to be a
drawn face: where one is missing the browser synthesises it, and
synthesised weights look noticeably worse. 400 and 500 are safe
everywhere; verify 600 on the platforms you support.

## What is not here

**A metric role for large figures.** Its sizes would be identical to three
of the heading steps; the real difference is tabular figures, which
`font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` already covers. There is no stat
component yet, so it would be a role nothing reads.

**A code role.** Same size as `--text-body-sm`, differing only by family.
`var(--font-mono)` covers it until a Code component exists.

## Customization

The family is a token like any other:

```css
:root {
  --font-sans: 'Geist Variable', system-ui, sans-serif;
  --font-heading: 'Newsreader Variable', Georgia, serif; /* serif headings */
}
```

Every rule that reads `var(--font-sans)` picks it up with no component
change — which is all of them, because components set the family
explicitly rather than inheriting it from the page. Re-check the weights when you do — a real typeface
usually ships fewer weights than the four above, or different ones.

To move the scale itself rather than the face, override the role tokens
directly — each is a `--text-<role>` and its `--leading-<role>` partner.

foundations-spacing--docs.content:
import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as SpacingStories from './Spacing.stories'

<Meta of={SpacingStories} />

# Spacing

Pick a spacing token by **what the gap does**, not by its size. Six roles
cover every gap and pad in the kit, and each role has one value. A
designer never chooses between 12 and 16 pixels: they choose
`--space-cluster` or `--space-group`.

<Canvas of={SpacingStories.Roles} />

## The six roles

| Token | Use for | Value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--space-stack` | Lines of text under each other: title to description, label to value | 4 |
| `--space-inline` | Small things side by side: icon to text, label to value on one line, breadcrumb items | 8 |
| `--space-cluster` | Controls or parts that sit together: filters in a toolbar, an avatar to its content, the parts of a page heading, inside a small card | 12 |
| `--space-group` | Items and blocks that belong together: cards in a row, toolbar to table, table cell sides | 16 |
| `--space-container` | Inside the edge of a card, panel or page heading | 24 |
| `--space-section` | Page edge and between page sections | 24 |

The scale is short on purpose: 4, 8, 12, 16, 24. Section and container
share 24px, so separate sections with a card edge or a rule, not with
extra white space. Apply `--space-section` to the page edge from 64rem
up; below that, keep the edge at its narrow value.

The numeric steps (`--space-0-5` to `--space-20`) still exist for the few
places no role fits, such as the size of an icon disc.

## Controls

The control tier binds a control's height, padding and icon gap, so a
control never reads a spacing role for its own box.

| Control token | lg | md | sm | xs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--control-{tier}` height | 40 | 32 | 24 | 20 |
| `--control-{tier}-pad` (rows, menu items) | – | 10 | 8 | 6 |
| `--control-{tier}-pad-spacious` (buttons, from the outer edge to the label) | – | 12 | 12 | 6 |
| `--control-{tier}-gap` (icon to label) | – | 6 | 6 | 4 |

A field is `lg` tall by default and `md` at `size="sm"`, one step above a
button. It takes the numeric step `--space-1-5` (6px) inside its edge at
both sizes, and `--space-stack` between its label, box and helper text.

A small control inside a component (a table's sort button, a modal's
close button, a badge, the number input's steppers) reads the control tier
of its own size, like any other control, not a spacing role.

## One scale

The kit has one set of numbers: there is no density mode and no scaling
factor. Where a screen needs a tighter control, such as a button in a
table row or a filter in a toolbar, use that component's `size="sm"`.

## Touch and rem

Controls are below the 44px touch minimum on purpose: on coarse pointers
every control widens its hit area to 44px without growing the box. Every
value is in `rem`, so it follows the user's root font size; "32px" is 32px
at the default 16px root.

foundations-breakpoints--docs.content:
import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as BreakpointsStories from './Breakpoints.stories'

<Meta of={BreakpointsStories} />

# Breakpoints

Five breakpoints, inherited from the underlying CSS framework without
modification. Zweihänder declares no `--breakpoint-*` of its own.

| Prefix | Min width | At a 16px root |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *(none)* | `0` | 0px |
| `sm:` | `40rem` | 640px |
| `md:` | `48rem` | 768px |
| `lg:` | `64rem` | 1024px |
| `xl:` | `80rem` | 1280px |
| `2xl:` | `96rem` | 1536px |

<Canvas of={BreakpointsStories.Scale} />

The box below reports the breakpoint currently in effect. Resize the
preview — or use Storybook's viewport toolbar — and it changes.

<Canvas of={BreakpointsStories.Active} />

## They are min-width, and that has a direction

`md:flex` means "flex at 768px **and above**". There is no maximum, so
rules outside a media query are the small-screen case and every
`@media (width >= …)` is an override for larger screens. Write the phone
layout first and widen it; writing the desktop layout first means every
breakpoint has to undo something.

The other direction is expressible — `@media (width < 48rem)` caps a rule
below a breakpoint — but mixing both in one component is where responsive
CSS usually becomes unreadable. Pick min-width and stay there.

## Breakpoints are in rem

`40rem`, not `640px`. A reader who raises their browser's default font
size gets the layout to break earlier, because the layout responds to how
large the text actually is rather than to the device. That is the correct
behaviour and it is worth not overriding: a `px` breakpoint holds a
multi-column layout together long after its text has stopped fitting.

The px column above is only true at the default 16px root.

## The kit has no opinion yet

**No component here uses a breakpoint.** Controls such as Button and Text
Input are inline-sized — they fill whatever their container gives them and have no
layout of their own to rearrange. The stories on this page are the only
responsive code in the repo.

That is expected: breakpoints are a **layout** concern, and the kit ships
components, not page layouts. Marketing sections, dashboards and checkout
flows are where these will actually get used, and where the kit will need an opinion about
which of the five are load-bearing. Most design systems end up leaning on
two or three.

## Container queries are usually the better tool

A breakpoint asks how wide the *viewport* is. A component almost always
wants to know how wide **its own container** is — the same card is narrow
in a sidebar and wide in a main column at one identical viewport width.

Container queries are in every current browser, and they are plain CSS:

```css
.card {
  container-type: inline-size;
}

.cardBody {
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;
}

@container (width >= 28rem) {
  .cardBody {
    flex-direction: row;
  }
}
```

When a component is built here that needs to reflow, it should reach for
`@container` first and a viewport breakpoint only when the thing being
arranged really is the page.

## Customization

Breakpoints are theme keys like any other, redefined in the `@theme`
block:

```css
@theme {
  --breakpoint-sm: 30rem;
  --breakpoint-3xl: 120rem;
}
```

Two cautions. These generate utility *variants*, so they cannot be
overridden per-scope by `Theme` the way a color can — a variant is
compiled into a media query at build time, and there is no runtime
variable to swap. And removing a default breakpoint removes its prefix
entirely, so any existing `lg:` becomes a silent no-op rather than an
error.

foundations-radius--docs.content:
import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as RadiusStories from './Radius.stories'

<Meta of={RadiusStories} />

# Radius

Rounding is a **single setting**, not a value picked per component. A
`radius` preset on `Theme` rescales everything inside it at once, and
components follow because they reference an *intent* — control, field,
panel — rather than a fixed number.

```tsx
<Theme radius="full-rounded">
  <Button>Pill</Button>
</Theme>
```

## Presets

Three: `sharp`, **`rounded` (the default)**, `full-rounded`. The
default is set by `--radius-factor: 1` and `--radius-full: 0px` on
`:root`, which is exactly what the `rounded` preset writes — so a scope
with no `radius` prop and a scope with `radius="rounded"` are identical.

<Canvas of={RadiusStories.Presets} />

Look at the `full-rounded` row. **The button becomes a pill; the input and the
panel get rounder but stop short of one.** That is the whole reason this
is a system rather than a number: a fully rounded text field reads as a
search pill in a form that isn't one, and a fully rounded card stops
looking like a container. Only controls opt all the way in.

`sharp` flattens every corner in the scope to `0`, including panels.

## How it works

Three variables do the work, all on `:root`:

| Variable | Default | Set by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--radius` | `0.375rem` | you, for the `md` step |
| `--radius-factor` | `1` | the `radius` preset |
| `--radius-full` | `0px` | the `radius` preset, only at `full-rounded` |

Six steps are cut from the base, after Atlassian's shape scale: `xs` a
third (2px), `sm` two thirds (4px), `md` the base (6px), `lg` four thirds
(8px), `xl` twice (12px) and `2xl` eight thirds (16px). Every step is
multiplied by the factor, so the preset scales the whole scale rather
than replacing it:

| Preset | Factor | `--radius-full` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `sharp` | `0` | `0px` |
| `rounded` | `1` | `0px` |
| `full-rounded` | `1.5` | `9999px` |

The pill is a `max()`. `--radius-control` resolves to
`max(step, var(--radius-full))` — normally the step wins because
`--radius-full` is `0px`, and at the `full-rounded` preset the `9999px` wins
instead.

Fields and panels use the same shape with a ceiling wrapped around it:

```css
max(step, min(cap, var(--radius-full)))
```

`min(cap, --radius-full)` is `0px` normally and the cap at `full-rounded`, so they
step up with the preset and stop there. Concretely, at the default base:

| Preset | `control` | `field` | `panel` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sharp` | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| `rounded` | 6px | 6px | 12px |
| `full-rounded` | pill | 12px | 24px |

The default input is 40px tall, so a pill would be 20px. `field` at
`full-rounded` lands under that on purpose, and a test asserts it.

## Two rules

### 1. Radius is tier × intent

A control's corner is not picked per component. Its **size tier** picks
the step, and its **intent** picks what happens at `full-rounded`:

| Tier | Step | Control (pill at `full-rounded`) | Field (stops one step up) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `xs` (20px) | `--radius-sm` | `--control-xs-radius` | `--control-xs-radius-field` |
| `sm` (24px) | `--radius-sm` | `--control-sm-radius` | `--control-sm-radius-field` |
| `md` (32px) | `--radius-md` | `--control-md-radius` = `--radius-control` | `--control-md-radius-field` = `--radius-field` |

The small tiers take the smaller step because the same corner on a box
two thirds the height reads as a pill. `--radius-xs` (2px) is for marks
smaller than a control: a checkbox box, a badge, a key cap. See
[Sizing](?path=/docs/foundations-sizing--docs) for which component reads
which tier.

### 2. Nested corners are the outer corner minus the inset

When a rounded thing sits inside another, with an even inset, its corner
is the container's minus that inset, never its own token:

```css
.menu {
  --menu-inset: var(--space-1);
  padding: var(--menu-inset);
  border-radius: var(--radius-field);
}
.menu-item {
  border-radius: calc(var(--radius-field) - var(--menu-inset));
}
```

The pills Tabs chips work this way: their corner is the track's minus the
2px track inset. Menu no longer does: its popup is inset 12px, further than
its 8px corner, so an item is a free-standing shape with the control
radius, and the `.menu` above is an illustration only. A negative
result clamps to 0, so a square container gets square children. Both
corners then stay concentric at every preset; two independent tokens only
line up at one.

The rule is for concentric shapes. A close button 12px inside a popover's
corner is a free-standing control, not a nested shape, and keeps its own
step.

## Always round: `--radius-pill`

`--radius-pill` is `9999px` at every preset. It is for things that are
round by nature, not by preset: a badge count, an avatar, a switch track,
a slider thumb, a spinner. `--radius-full` is the preset's pill switch:
read directly it is `0` everywhere except `radius="full-rounded"`.

## Intent tokens

What components actually use.

<Canvas of={RadiusStories.Intent} />

| Token | Used by | Pills at `full-rounded` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--radius-control` | the md tier of Button, ToggleButton, Tabs, Pagination | yes |
| `--radius-field` | every field | no |
| `--radius-panel` | Modal | no |

Surfaces that float or frame content without being a dialog read a step,
`--radius-lg` (8px): Card, Popover, Menu, the Select and Combobox lists,
the date picker, Toast and Alert. They follow the preset's factor and never
become a pill.

A new control or field should pick the intent that matches its shape, not
a step.
Getting this wrong is invisible at the default preset and only shows up
when someone sets `radius="full-rounded"` — which is exactly the kind of bug a
token system exists to prevent.

## Steps

The raw scale — `--radius-xs` through `--radius-2xl` — for anything that is
genuinely decorative rather than a control, field or panel.

<Canvas of={RadiusStories.Steps} />

These follow the preset like everything else, so a decorative corner in
application code stays in step with the controls beside it.

A genuinely circular element uses `--radius-pill` (see above), not
`--radius-full`.

## Scoping and overriding

Presets nest, and `Theme` takes a `render` prop, so a single component can
opt out without a wrapper element:

```tsx
<Theme radius="full-rounded" render={<Button />}>
  Just this one is a pill
</Theme>
```

For a value the presets don't cover, set the variables directly — `tokens`
is applied after the preset, so it wins:

```tsx
<Theme radius="rounded" tokens={{ 'radius-factor': '2.4' }}>
```

Globally, change the base in CSS and leave the factor to the presets:

```css
:root {
  --radius: 1rem;
}
```

## One caveat about the base

The steps are ratios of the base, so they keep their proportions when the
base moves, but small bases round down: at `--radius: 0.1875rem` (3px)
`xs` is 1px and `sm` 2px. Prefer moving the preset over moving the base.

foundations-shadows--docs.content:
import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as ShadowsStories from './Shadows.stories'

<Meta of={ShadowsStories} />

# Shadows

Elevation has two levels and an off switch, after Atlassian's elevation
model. Each resolves per appearance rather than being a fixed value.

<Canvas of={ShadowsStories.Scale} />

| Token | Use for | Light |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--shadow-none` | Turning elevation off | `0 0 #0000` |
| `--shadow-raised` | A surface that can be picked up and moved, such as a card being dragged | `0 1px 1px` 25% over a 1px edge at 31% |
| `--shadow-overlay` | Anything that floats above the page: menus, popovers, modals, toasts | `0 8px 12px` 15% over a 1px edge at 31% |

Each level is two layers: a soft directional layer that says how far the
surface floats, over a 1px ambient edge that keeps its outline when the
surface behind it is the same colour.

**A surface that stays put needs no shadow.** It separates from the page
by its surface and its border. Controls are flat: buttons and fields
carry borders, not shadows. Card's `elevated` appearance is the one
resting surface on `raised`, and lifts to `overlay` on hover when
clickable.

The seven step names from before (`--shadow-2xs` to `--shadow-2xl`) still
resolve: `2xs`, `xs` and `sm` read `raised`; `md`, `lg`, `xl` and `2xl`
read `overlay`. Use the two level names in new styles.

`--shadow-none` exists so that turning elevation off is a token rather
than a literal. `box-shadow: none` also works, but it cannot be swapped by
a `Theme` and it breaks a transition between two shadow states — `0 0
#0000` interpolates, `none` does not.

## Dark mode is derived, not retyped

Only the light values are written down. The dark ones are **computed from
them**: every alpha is multiplied by 4 and clamped at 0.6.

<Canvas of={ShadowsStories.Modes} />

A drop shadow works by darkening what is under it, and a dark page has
almost nothing left to darken. So the multiplier spends a small budget
well; it does not rescue dark mode.

**In dark mode, surface lightness is the primary elevation signal and the
shadow is a secondary cue.** In light mode it is the other way around. If
you are building a floating surface and it does not read as raised in dark
mode, reach for a lighter surface token, not a heavier shadow.

Deriving rather than retyping means editing a level edits both modes, and
the `Modes` story asserts the two did not collapse into the same value.

## A note on rings and shadows

`box-shadow` is a single property, so a shadow and a focus ring drawn the
same way would overwrite each other — which is why systems that draw rings
with `box-shadow` need machinery to compose the two.

The kit sidesteps it: focus is drawn with `outline`, which has its own
property and its own `outline-offset`, and current browsers follow
`border-radius` with it. An elevated surface can carry a shadow and a
focus ring at once, and neither needs to know about the other.

## What is not here

**Inset shadows.** For recessed wells and pressed states. They are a real
gap, but the kit has no recessed surface and no pressed treatment yet, so
they would be a step nothing reads. Add them as `elevation-inset-*` in `tokens/semantic.json` when
the first one lands; the alpha derivation applies unchanged.

**Coloured shadows.** A shadow tinted toward the accent instead of black.
Worth having, but it needs a real decision about which token it reads and
how it behaves in dark mode, not a mechanical port.

## Customization

The raw values are `--elevation-raised` and `--elevation-overlay` in
`:root` and `.dark`; the `*` block maps them onto `--shadow-*` and does not need to
change.

Change a level by editing `tokens/semantic.json` and running `npm run
tokens` — light and dark regenerate together. Overriding `--shadow-overlay`
directly on a `Theme` scope also works and skips the derivation, which is
the right tool for a one-off surface and the wrong one for changing the
scale.

foundations-focus--docs.content:
import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as FocusStories from './Focus.stories'

<Meta of={FocusStories} />

# Focus

One ring for the whole kit: `outline: var(--focus-width) solid var(--color-border-focused)`,
shown on `:focus-visible` only. Its colour is `--color-border-focused`, measured at 3:1
against the page (see [Colors](?path=/docs/foundations-colors--docs)).

<Canvas of={FocusStories.Rings} />

## Outside or inside

There are two offsets and the choice is mechanical.

**`--focus-offset`** draws the ring outside the element. It is the default
for anything that stands on its own: buttons, fields, links, checkboxes.

**`--focus-offset-inset`** draws it inside. Use it when the element sits
flush against the edge of a container that clips its overflow, or when an
outside ring would run into a neighbour: tabs, table rows and sortable
headers, the close button in a modal, popover, alert
or toast, the remove button in a tag, the steppers in a number input.

A third value is a smell. The one exception is a selected colour swatch,
which already carries a selection ring at `--focus-offset`, so its focus
ring sits one pixel further out to stay visible.

## Why the ring is in pixels

`--focus-width` and both offsets are plain pixels, not `rem`. A ring is a
stroke, and WCAG 2.4.13 measures it in CSS pixels.

foundations-motion--docs.content:
import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as MotionStories from './Motion.stories'

<Meta of={MotionStories} />

# Motion

Three transition durations and one spinner speed. Every `transition` in the
kit reads one of them; nothing types a number of milliseconds.

<Canvas of={MotionStories.Durations} />

## Choosing a step

The step follows what moves, not how important it is. A popup appearing
is `fast`: it answers a click, and anything slower reads as lag. A colour
or state change is `base`. Something that travels across the screen (the
tab indicator, a toast, a progress bar's fill) is `slow`, because the eye has to follow
it. If a new transition does not fit one of the three, that is a reason to
question the transition before adding a fourth step.

Easing is the browser default (`ease`) except where something grows or
shrinks: Collapse opens with `ease-out`, so the panel arrives
fast and settles. There is no easing token: two curves, each with an
obvious owner, do not need a name yet.

## Reduced motion

Under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` the three transition steps resolve to
`0ms` in `tokens.css`, so every transition in the kit stops in one place
without each component repeating a media query.

Two things are exempt. Toast swaps its slide for a 200ms fade, written as
a number on purpose, since the tokens would turn the fade into a jump.
And spinners: a stopped spinner says nothing is happening, so instead of
stopping they slow from `--duration-spin` to `--duration-spin-reduced`.
Each spinner opts into that itself.

Loop animations with their own rhythm (the skeleton pulse, the
indeterminate progress bar) keep their own timing: they are a single
animation each, not a step anyone else should reuse.

import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as LayeringStories from './Layering.stories'

<Meta of={LayeringStories} />

# Layering

Four layers for everything that leaves the page flow. A component picks
the layer by what it is, never by trying a bigger number.

<Canvas of={LayeringStories.Layers} />

## One layer for every overlay

Popovers, menus, listboxes, date pickers and modals all share
`--layer-overlay`. They are portalled to the end of `<body>`, so at an equal
z-index the one opened last paints on top: a Select opened inside a Modal
lands above the Modal without either knowing about the other. Giving the
Modal a higher layer would break exactly that case.

Tooltips sit one layer up because they can belong to anything, including a
trigger inside an open overlay. Toasts sit above everything: a toast raised
while a modal is open still has to be read.

## Local z-index

A value used only to order parts inside one component (a table's sticky
header at `1`, the tab indicator at `-1`) is local and stays a plain number.
Keep these at single digits so they stay well below `--layer-sticky`.

foundations-cursors--docs.content:
import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as CursorsStories from './Cursors.stories'

<Meta of={CursorsStories} />

# Cursors

Three tokens, and a convention that surprises most people: **buttons do
not get `cursor: pointer`. Links do.**

## The convention

`cursor: pointer` means "this navigates" — it is the hand that appears
over a link. Browsers have never applied it to `<button>`, `<select>` or a
checkbox, and neither does this kit. Interactive elements that act on the
current page keep the regular arrow; only a link gets the hand. This is a
deliberate departure from the very common `button { cursor: pointer }`
reset.

It is worth knowing the argument on the other side: a large body of
usability opinion holds that the hand cursor is now such a widespread
affordance for "clickable" that removing it costs more than the semantic
purity gains. If your product takes that view, this is a one-line change —
see **Customization** below. The point of making it a token is that it is
one line, in one place, rather than a decision re-litigated per component.

<Canvas of={CursorsStories.Tokens} />

## `--cursor-button`

`default` — the regular arrow. Applied by Button.

Note this changes nothing visually today: a native `<button>` already
shows the arrow. **The token's job is not its current value; it is that
the value is reachable.** Without it, switching the kit to `pointer` means
editing every component; with it, it is one declaration.

## `--cursor-link`

`pointer` — the hand.

This one exists because the convention above has a second half that is
easy to state and easy to get wrong. Button takes `href`, so it can
render as a real `<a href>` — and when it did, it inherited
`--cursor-button` and lost the hand that the browser gives every other
link on the page. A link styled as a button is still a link.

```css
a[href].button {
  cursor: var(--cursor-link);
}
```

The `a[href]` part is doing real work. An `<a>` without `href` is not a
link and browsers do not give it the hand either, so matching on the
attribute rather than the element keeps the rule honest.

The distinction the kit draws is navigation versus action, not
appearance: a `<button>` styled as a link would still act on the current
page, so it would keep the arrow.

| | Element | Cursor |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `<Button>` | `<button>` | arrow |
| `<Button href="/x">` | `<a href>` | hand |

The Button `Href` story asserts this, and compares against a bare
`<a href>` rather than the literal `pointer` — so overriding
`--cursor-link` moves the assertion with it instead of breaking it.

## `--cursor-disabled`

`not-allowed` — used by TextInput, and **not** by Button. That asymmetry
is not an oversight.

A disabled `<input>` stays hit-testable, so a cursor set on it renders and
the user gets feedback on hover. Button's disabled state is
`pointer-events: none`, which makes the element untargetable; an
untargetable element is never hovered, so a cursor there would be dead
CSS. The `pointer-events: none` is not incidental — because Button
can render as an `<a>`, which ignores the `disabled` attribute entirely. Blocking pointer events is what actually disables it
in that case.

So the token applies to the pattern where a control stays hoverable while
disabled — including a control deliberately wrapped so a tooltip can
explain *why*. That trade-off, between a disabled control you can
interrogate and one that is inert, is a real design choice, and the two
components here happen to sit on opposite sides of it.

## Adding tokens

A mature system ends up with a token per interactive component —
checkboxes, menu items, radios, switches, slider thumbs. This kit has
three, because it has two components and one of them can render as two
different things.

{/* docs:check allow --cursor-slider-thumb -- an example of a token not to add */}

**Add a token when the component that needs it is built, not before.** A
`--cursor-slider-thumb` with no Slider is a value nobody can verify and
that the eventual Slider may not want.

## Customization

All three are plain CSS keywords, not colors, so they override like any
other custom property:

```css
:root {
  --cursor-button: pointer;
}
```

Load any override after Zweihänder's own stylesheet so the cascade picks it
up. Setting `--cursor-button: pointer` is the one-line version of adopting
the mainstream convention; it leaves `--cursor-link` alone, which is
already `pointer`, so the two simply converge.

foundations-sizing--docs.content:
import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as SizingStories from './Sizing.stories'

<Meta of={SizingStories} />

# Sizing

Every control's geometry comes from two facts: its **size tier** and its
**intent**. The tier binds height, inline padding, the gap between icon and
label, the icon and the corner. The intent (control or field) decides
three things only: how tall it is at a given `size` (a field is one step
taller than a button), which padding it takes, and whether it becomes a
pill at `radius="full-rounded"`.

<Canvas of={SizingStories.Tiers} />

The table reads each token back from the page, so it shows what the
current radius preset resolves to. `lg` is a height only: it is the
default field, which takes the `md` gap, icon and field radius.

## The box ramp

Every element is a box, and every box with a fixed height or a fixed
square stands on a step of one ramp. The same role always takes the same
step, so a close button is 24px in a Modal and in a Toast, and a nav
item is as tall as the button beside it.

<Canvas of={SizingStories.BoxRamp} />

`md` (32px) is the default. The control tiers below are the ramp's `xs`,
`sm`, `md` and `lg` under another name.

### Which step a role takes

| Role | Step | Size |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The default field (`size="md"`) and an OTP cell | `lg` | 40px |
| The default control: button, tab, pagination and menu item, calendar day, a nav item; a field at `size="sm"` | `md` | 32px |
| A small inline control; a button inside a field (clear, calendar, stepper); a close button inside a surface (Modal, Popover, Toast, Alert); the small Stepper marker; the medium spinner | `sm` | 24px |
| Small parts: Tag `size="sm"`, the slider thumb, Kbd `md`, a file icon | `xs` | 20px |
| A mark that sits with a glyph: the checkbox and radio box, Badge `md`, Kbd `sm`, the small slider thumb, the small spinner, a skeleton line | `2xs` | 16px |
| A leading visual: Avatar `lg`, the small EmptyState icon | `lg` | 40px |
| A large visual: the Stats icon, the EmptyState icon | `xl` | 48px |
| A glyph inside a control | `--icon-{tier}` | 12 / 14 / 16px |
| A glyph inside a md Button or ToggleButton | `--icon-lg` | 20px, box stays 32px |
| A line of text, and an icon beside it | `--leading-*` × `--text-*` | one line |
| A table or list row | `box-md` + 2 × `--space-inline` | 48px |

The rules that go with the table:

- **A component picks the step by role.** Whoever uses the component
  picks only its `size`, and `size` points at a step.
- **Composite boxes take no free number.** A row, a Tag or a top bar is
  the box inside it plus a spacing role on each side: `--row-height` is
  `box-md` plus `--space-inline` above and below (48px). Text boxes
  are a line tall (`--leading-*` × `--text-*`); an icon beside text sits
  in a box one line tall.
- **A box that grows with its content** uses `min-block-size` at a step,
  never `block-size`.
- **A box with a fixed size and padding or a border declares
  `box-sizing: border-box` itself.** The kit ships no global reset, so
  the app's own CSS decides the default.

Off the ramp, each for a reason: 1–2px strokes, dots and bars under
12px (radio dot, Badge dot, progress bar), switch track widths, region
sizes (ColorPicker, a vertical Slider, overlay widths), the 44px touch
target and icons sized in `em` inside text. `npm run tokens` stops when a
control, size or row token leaves the ramp without a
listed reason, and when `--row-height` stops being the sum above.

## Who reads which tier

| Tier | Height | Components |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `lg` | 40px | every field at its default `size="md"`: TextInput, Search, Select, Combobox, NumberInput, DatePicker, DateRangePicker, and the cells of OTPInput |
| `md` | 32px | the default: Button, ToggleButton, Tabs, Pagination, Menu item; and every field at `size="sm"` |
| `sm` | 24px | the small inline size of Button, ToggleButton and Tabs, the Menubar trigger, and a button inside a field |
| `xs` | 20px | compact parts only: Tag, the slider thumb |

The checkbox and radio box, the switch tracks, Badge and Avatar have
their own size tokens (`--choice-box`, `--switch-md-w`, `--badge-md`,
`--avatar-md`).

A component's `size` prop points at a tier; the names need not match. A
field's `md` reads tier `lg` and its `sm` reads tier `md`, because a field
is one step taller than the button beside it.

**A field is one step taller than a button**, after Atlassian Design. A
field's `md` reads `--control-lg` (40px) and its `sm` reads `--control-md`
(32px), so a `sm` field lines up with a default Button in a toolbar.
There is no 24px field. Textarea has no height token: its block padding
puts one line of text at the same two heights.

**Buttons and fields have no `xs`.** A 20px button reads as a part,
not a control.

**The 24px floor is for the hit area, not the drawn box.** WCAG 2.5.8
asks for a 24×24px target. A box drawn smaller (the checkbox is
16px) keeps its look and widens its hit area to 24px with a
`::before`. On touch screens every tier grows its hit area to
`--target-coarse` (44px) the same way, without growing the visible box.

## Intent

**Padding.** Rows and menu items take `pad`, because their text is left
aligned. Buttons take `pad-spacious`: a centred label reads as cramped
with less. The two only differ at `md` (10 against 12px); at `sm` and `xs`
there is no room to spend. A field takes neither: 6px (`--space-1-5`)
inside its edge at both sizes, Atlassian's field padding, so the value
sits close under the label above it.

**Radius.** The tier picks the step (`--radius-sm` for `xs` and `sm`,
`--radius-md` for `md`, so a short box does not read as a pill by
accident). The intent picks what happens at `radius="full-rounded"`:
`--control-{tier}-radius` becomes a pill, `--control-{tier}-radius-field`
stops one step up. At `md` these are exactly `--radius-control` and
`--radius-field`. A field reads `--control-md-radius-field` at both sizes.
See [Radius](?path=/docs/foundations-radius--docs).

<Canvas of={SizingStories.SameTier} />

A default Button beside a text field and a select at `size="sm"`: one
height (32px), one corner, one type size. The story asserts all three,
and the icons: 20px in the Button, 16px for a field's own icon and for a
picker's chevron. At the same `size` the field is the taller one: a
default field is 40px.

## Why these gaps

The gap is 4px at `xs` and 6px at `sm` and `md`. Before tiers each
component chose its own, and they disagreed at the small size: Button and
the field put 8px between icon and label, Tag put 4px. One 6px gap for the
two sizes most of an interface uses ends that; the compact `xs` parts keep
4px. A field reads the `md` gap and the `md` icon at both of its sizes.
